about: Brotherhood calls itself America’s oldest winery, and the claim rests on a long, unbroken record. John Jaques, a cobbler in Washingtonville in the Hudson Valley, planted native grapes behind his store around 1824 and released his first commercial vintage in 1839, initially as sacramental wine for his Presbyterian church. In 1886 New York wine merchants J. M. Emerson & Son bought the business and named it Brotherhood, adding stone buildings and the underground vaults that still lie beneath the property. The winery survived Prohibition by making sacramental and medicinal wine.

In 1987 winemaker Cesar Baeza and partners began a premium line of single-variety wines, and since 2005 the winery has been owned with the Chadwick and Castro families, who have roots in Chile’s Maule Valley. Brotherhood buys grapes from independent growers in the Finger Lakes, on Long Island and elsewhere in New York, choosing fruit that suits each wine. The Premium Selection Dry Rosé is made in a crisp, dry style, with wild strawberry, red cherry and watermelon on the nose and red berries, cranberry and pink grapefruit on the palate.
facts: Grapes bought from independent New York State growers
Founded 1839 (first commercial vintage); on the National Register of Historic Places
